lines: Every signal anyone was watching stayed green, right up until the disk itself ran out of room.
That gap between what the dashboard showed and what actually happened is the whole reason this incident is worth studying closely.
A slot doesn't report its own danger anywhere a status page checks. It just sits there, pinning exactly what it was built to pin.
Before I show you what actually happened here, answer this.
That connector never crashed. It never lost its connection. By every normal measure, it was healthy the whole weekend.
Can a connector that looks completely healthy still be the reason a disk fills up like that?
answer: Saying no treats being connected and being healthy as the same thing as actually making progress. They aren't.
A slot only moves forward when its consumer confirms a new position, and a consumer watching a quiet table simply has nothing new to confirm, no matter how healthy it otherwise looks.

lines: Here's why a slot can sit frozen for an entire weekend without anyone noticing.
A replication slot survives a crash on purpose, and it was designed to know nothing about whether its own consumer is still there.
With no reader at all, there's simply nothing telling the server it's safe to let go of anything that slot might still need.
I ran that exact scenario against this sandbox's own real database, not a simulation of it.
A slot with no reader at all, under a real batch of writes, and I read its retained log size before and after.
The gap came back larger every single time, because nothing about having no reader ever lets that gap shrink on its own.
Now here's the fix, and it's not what you'd expect from the word running.
I split the identical amount of writing into five separate pieces. One slot's own consumer never once confirmed between those pieces.
The other slot's consumer confirmed after every single piece, the exact same way a heartbeat would, even with no real change worth capturing.
I measured both of those slots side by side, against the identical total amount of writing.
The slot that was never confirmed finished with a large, lingering gap behind it.
The slot that confirmed after every piece finished with a gap so much smaller it barely counted. Confirming, not merely running, is what actually moves the marker.
A slot that never lets go can obviously fill a disk eventually. So what's the actual safety valve for that?
You can set a real limit on how much log a slot is allowed to hold onto.
Past that limit, the server is finally allowed to remove log the slot still needed, which is exactly the trade it sounds like.
I set that exact limit on a real slot on this sandbox, then wrote past it on purpose.
Before crossing the limit, the slot's own status read back as perfectly fine, holding exactly what it was supposed to hold.
After crossing it, the status flipped to lost, and trying to read from that slot afterward got refused outright, by the database itself, not by anything I wrote.
Step back, and the whole weekend-long incident comes down to three separate, measurable facts.

A slot with nobody reading it pins log space no matter how healthy its connector looks. A confirmed read, not uptime, is the only thing that actually frees that space. And the safety valve that caps it trades a full disk for a broken stream.
None of those three facts shows up anywhere on a typical connector status dashboard.
Here's the one question none of that has actually answered yet.
If connector status can't catch this, what number should someone actually be watching for, before the disk gets anywhere near full?
answer: Saying connector status is enough ignores the entire weekend you just watched happen while that status read healthy the whole time.
The number worth watching is the retained log gap itself, read straight from the slot's own position, because that's the exact thing that was filling the disk the whole time.
